cues.txt: Process control is sometimes called analog control
because it involves controlling analog loops, like the temperature of a tank.
And at the heart of almost every one of those loops is a PID controller.
In this video, I'll explain how PID control works, what it means to tune a PID loop,
and how to choose the right control mode for your process.
By the end of the video, you will know:
How a PID loop works, and what the proportional, integral,
and derivative parts each do,
What tuning a PID loop actually means,
The difference between open-loop and closed-loop tuning,
and When to use proportional-only, PI, or full PID control.
Let's start with the control loop itself,
because everything else in this video builds on it.
To understand how a control loop works, let’s look at the practical example of
controlling the temperature of liquid in a tank.
A temperature sensor measures the temperature of the tank.
That measurement is compared to the setpoint by the control device.
Based on that comparison, the control device sends out a control signal
that adjusts a steam valve,
and the steam valve changes the temperature inside the tank.
Then the sensor measures the temperature again, and the whole cycle repeats.
Closing loops like this is the heart of process control.
So what actually decides how far to open or close that valve?
That's the job of the PID algorithm.
The PID control algorithm runs inside the control device,
and its job is to calculate the control variable, also called the control output.
That control output is what governs how far to open or close the valve.

PID stands for proportional, integral, and derivative.
These are the three parts of the equation that determine the control output,
based on the difference between the setpoint and the current state of the process.
That difference is called the error.
Each part has its own gain factor: Kp for the proportional part,
Ki for the integral part, and Kd for the derivative part.
This gain defines how strong the reaction of the controller
will be in response to an error.
Generally speaking, the proportional part
makes sure disturbances are reacted to quickly.
The integral part makes sure there is little or no steady-state offset
between the desired and the actual values.
And the derivative part minimizes overshoot and oscillation
as the controller drives the process variable toward the setpoint.
All three create their output based on the measured error
of the process being regulated.
When a loop is working properly, any error caused by a setpoint change
or a process disturbance is quickly eliminated by the three parts working together.
Let's look at what each one actually contributes,
starting with the proportional factor.
Proportional is the easiest of the three to understand.
The output of the proportional factor
is simply the gain multiplied by the measured error.
So a larger proportional gain, or a larger error,
makes for a greater output from the proportional factor.
There are two things to watch out for.
The first is that if you set the proportional gain too high,
the controller repeatedly overshoots the setpoint, which leads to oscillation.
The second is that when the error becomes very small,
the loop output becomes negligible.
This is the real limitation of a proportional-only loop,
because even once it reaches steady state, there is still some error left over.
So how do we get rid of that leftover error?
That's what the integral factor is for.
Think of the integral factor as a basket
that the loop stores all of its measured error in.
Positive error is added to positive error, and negative error
is added to negative error.
Sometimes the basket empties out, like when positive error is added to negative error,
or the other way around.
When the integral factor is working properly, that basket stays nearly empty.
The integral factor is important because even when the error is so small that the
proportional factor is no longer effective, the integral is still working away,
collecting error until it is large enough to matter.
Eliminating that leftover steady-state offset is a big part of the integral's job.
In fact, most of the control loop's action at steady state
comes from the integral factor.
The downside is that if the integral gain is too large,
it will strongly contribute to overshooting the setpoint.
Derivative is the least understood, and the least used, of the three factors.
In fact, a majority of PID loops in the real world are really just PI loops,
using only the proportional and integral parts.
That said, there are certain applications where the derivative
plays a very important role.
Derivative action compensates for a changing error,
to hold back rapid changes in the control output.
When a load change or a setpoint change happens, the derivative action causes the
controller gain to move the opposite way as the measurement gets close to the setpoint.
This is often used to avoid overshoot and to further stabilize a loop.
By using all three parts together, process operators can:
Hold the process near the setpoint without major fluctuations,
using proportional control,
Eliminate offset, using integral control,
and Get a rapid response to major disturbances, using derivative control.
But not every process needs a full PID control strategy.
So which mode should you actually use?
Before we answer that, there are two terms you need to know.
Noise is temporary error readings
that don't reflect the true condition of the process variable.
Dead time is the amount of time delay between a disturbance
and the control action that responds to it.
Now here's a rough guide to which control mode you should use based on the
application requirements:
- Use proportional-only control when a small offset has no impact on the process.
- Use PI control when no offset can be tolerated, noise may be present,
and excessive dead time is not a problem.
- and Use full PID control when no offset can be tolerated,
there is no noise present, and dead time is an issue.
Regardless of the control mode that you use, to get a PID loop working optimally,
you need to tune the loop.
Let's talk about what that means in the next section.
Let's go back to our tank.
We're controlling the temperature in the vessel
by managing the flow of steam into its heating element.
Say we need to increase the temperature by 50 degrees Celsius.
How fast should we open the steam valve?
On one hand, time is money, so we want to raise the temperature as fast as we can.
On the other hand, if we significantly overshoot the setpoint,
we could ruin the product.
So how do we decide how much, and how fast, to open that valve?
The honest answer is that it depends.
It depends on the size of the vessel, the size of the steam valve,
the steam pressure, and other factors.
And that's the whole point of tuning: the control has to be matched
to the dynamics of the process.
So tuning is the methodology we use to calculate the gain factors,
so that we get more accurate and more stable control of the process variable.

Now let's look at how tuning is actually done.
Tuning methods fall into two general categories: open-loop and closed-loop.
Open-loop tuning is the simple, fast method.
You change the value of the control output by a fixed amount,
then watch how the system responds.
Because you're only changing the output, the system won't easily go out of control,
and if it starts to exceed any of your desired values,
you can quickly adjust the output back.
Closed-loop tuning is more complicated.
Here, you change the setpoint,
then analyze the performance of both the PID and the system.
This method is sometimes used to fine-tune a system
after you've already done open-loop tuning.
